subject: 함무라비 법비의 문체
title: A law code carved for everyone to see
content: A tall pillar of black stone, carved in the eighteenth century before our era, carries nearly three hundred rulings issued in the name of a Babylonian king. It stood in public where anybody could see it, and the text says explicitly that the wronged man should come before it and have his case read to him. This ancient monument has shaped how the era is understood. Its style is strikingly consistent. Almost every provision takes the same shape: a condition followed by a consequence, stating what happens if a particular situation arises. This form makes the text read as a list of decided cases rather than as a set of general principles, and scholars disagree about whether it functioned as enforceable law, as a record of royal justice, or as a monument advertising the king's virtue. Contemporary court records rarely cite it, which is one reason for the doubt. The provisions distinguish people by rank. Penalties for the same injury differ according to whether the victim was a free person, a dependent, or a slave, so the code records a stratified society while presenting itself as a guarantee of justice for all. Reading it therefore requires holding both facts together. Its most famous principle, that a like injury should be repaid in kind, was not universal even within the text, since compensation in silver appears frequently for the same offences committed against people of lower standing. The rhetoric surrounding the provisions is as revealing as the rulings. The prologue lists the cities the king restored and the temples he endowed, and the epilogue curses whoever effaces the inscription. What this civilization left is therefore not simply a legal document but an argument, in stone, that the ruler who commissioned it deserved to be remembered as the one who made the strong unable to oppress the weak.

subject: 트로이 발굴층의 혼란
title: Digging through nine cities at once
content: The mound at Hisarlik in north western Turkey contains the remains of at least nine successive settlements stacked on one another across more than three thousand years. Excavation there in the nineteenth century made the site famous, and it also produced one of the most instructive failures in the history of archaeology. The first excavator was searching for the city described in Homeric epic and dug a great trench straight down through the mound. Because he expected the ancient city to lie at the bottom, he cut through the intervening layers rapidly, destroying much of what stood between. The level he identified as the one he sought turned out to date roughly a thousand years too early, so the treasure he announced belonged to a civilization that had vanished long before the events the poems describe. Later work established the sequence properly. Careful attention to stratification, to pottery styles, and to the relation between walls and floors allowed the layers to be separated and dated, and a level showing destruction at roughly the right period was identified. Whether any historical siege corresponds to the poems remains disputed, and the evidence supports a destroyed city rather than a particular war. The methodological lesson entered the discipline permanently. Digging to reach an expected level destroys the evidence that would have tested the expectation, so excavation must proceed layer by layer with the record kept as the ground comes away. What is removed cannot be replaced, which makes archaeology unusual among sciences in that its central operation destroys its own material. The site itself is now a lesson as much as a monument. Visitors see a mound cut open, with the trench of the first excavation still visible, and the exposed section displays the successive centuries as clearly as any diagram could.

subject: 화산재 아래 남은 하루
title: A town stopped in the middle of an afternoon
content: When a volcano buried two towns on the Bay of Naples in the first century of our era, it preserved them in a way that no ordinary abandonment does. Places left gradually are stripped of anything valuable and then decay; these were sealed within hours, with everything in place, and the resulting record is the most detailed picture of daily life anywhere in the ancient Roman world. This ash preserved organic material as impressions. Where a body decayed inside the hardened deposit, a cavity remained, and although the method was crude, excavators in the nineteenth century learned to fill these cavities with plaster and recover the shape. The same method has recovered doors, shutters, furniture, and root systems of garden plants, so the layout of an ordinary household garden can be reconstructed species by species. What survives in these towns is emphatically ordinary. Bakeries hold loaves still in the oven, walls carry election notices and scratched insults, shops display counters with sunken jars, and one wall bears a schoolboy's alphabet. The written material on the walls is particularly valuable, since ancient literature preserves the language of the educated while these scratches preserve how people actually wrote when nobody was correcting them. Their excavation has itself become a historical problem. Early work was rapid and poorly recorded, objects were removed without noting where they lay, and exposure to weather has damaged painted surfaces that survived for eighteen centuries underground. Because future methods will recover more, a substantial portion of both sites is now deliberately left unexcavated. What this ancient disaster supplies is therefore a control against which the rest of Roman archaeology can be measured, since almost everywhere else the evidence has been filtered by what people chose to take with them.

subject: 병마용의 제작 공정
title: An army made on a production line
content: The pits near the tomb of the first emperor of a unified China hold thousands of life sized figures in fired clay, arranged in formation. Their scale attracts most attention, and the more informative discovery concerns how they were produced, since this ancient project required organising labour on a scale that few undertakings anywhere had matched. The figures were not individually sculpted. Bodies were assembled from standardised parts: legs built solid for stability, torsos formed as hollow shells, and arms and heads made separately and joined before firing. A limited number of head moulds supplied the basic form, after which features were modelled by hand, so the impression of individual portraits emerges from variation applied to a small set of templates. Ears, hair, and expression were finished separately on each figure. Inscriptions record the system. Names of foremen appear stamped or incised on many figures, and the same names recur across groups, which indicates that workshops were held responsible for what they produced. Such marking is a familiar device for quality control, and it allows modern researchers to reconstruct how the workforce was divided. Estimates suggest that many hundreds of workers were involved across a considerable period. The figures were originally painted in bright colour, most of which has been lost. Pigment survives only where conditions were right, and it deteriorates within minutes of exposure, so recent excavation proceeds with immediate conservation treatment. Several pits remain unopened for this reason. What the whole complex records about that era is the administrative capacity of a newly unified state. Producing, transporting, and installing an army of clay demanded the same coordination as any military campaign, and the emperor who ordered it was demonstrating exactly that.

subject: 사산 왕조의 은기
title: Silver plates that travelled further than the empire
content: The Sasanian empire, which held Persia and much of the surrounding region from the third century until the seventh, produced silver vessels of a distinctive kind. Shallow plates carry a hunting scene in raised relief, usually showing the king on horseback shooting an animal, and the pieces were made to be given rather than sold. Their distribution tells a story the written sources do not. Objects of this type have been recovered in large numbers far from the empire, particularly in the forested regions of northern Russia and Siberia, thousands of kilometres from where they were made. They reached those places through a chain of exchange, passing from hand to hand, and were eventually deposited in graves or hoards by people who had no connection to the ancient court that produced them. The imagery is remarkably consistent. The royal hunt appears again and again, with the ruler identified by an elaborate crown whose form differed for each king, which allows individual plates to be dated with unusual precision. This consistency was deliberate, since the objects functioned as statements about kingship and were distributed to allies, subordinates, and foreign courts as instruments of diplomacy. Analysis has complicated the picture. Some vessels turn out to be later copies made outside the empire by craftsmen imitating the style without understanding the details, so crowns appear that no king wore and scenes are assembled incorrectly. Distinguishing genuine court production from provincial imitation has occupied specialists for decades. What the plates finally demonstrate is how far an image can travel beyond the civilization that made it. The empire fell in the seventh century, and its royal iconography continued to be copied for generations afterwards by people who valued the objects without any interest in the monarchy they advertised.

subject: 아이슬란드 사가의 사실성
title: Stories written down three centuries later
content: The Icelandic sagas describe events of the ninth and tenth centuries — settlement, feuds, lawsuits, and voyages — in flat, unadorned prose that reads like reporting. They were written down in the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, and the gap between the events and the writing is the central problem for anybody using them as history. Their manner encourages trust. Characters are named with their genealogies, farms are located precisely in a landscape that still exists, and the narrative reports actions and speech without commenting on motive. Nothing in the style resembles legend. Yet the same style could equally be the achievement of skilled authors working in a tradition that valued exactly this restraint, and medieval writers elsewhere invented convincing detail readily. Independent evidence has settled some questions. Archaeology confirms the general pattern of settlement described, and excavation of a site on the coast of Newfoundland demonstrated that voyages to North America occurred, which several sagas describe. Ice cores and layers of volcanic ash allow certain events to be dated. On the other hand, particular conversations and individual killings cannot be checked by any method. Scholarly opinion has moved several times. An earlier generation treated the texts as reliable records preserved through oral tradition; a later one treated them as literary compositions of the era in which they were written; recent work occupies a middle position, allowing that oral tradition preserved a framework of names, places, and major events while the writing supplied the shape and much of the detail. What the debate illustrates is a difficulty common to any historical source that circulated before being fixed. The question is not whether the account is true or invented, but which layers within it come from which time, and answering that requires evidence from outside the text.

subject: 십자군 성채의 축성술
title: Castles built where two traditions met
content: The fortresses raised in the eastern Mediterranean during the medieval crusades are among the most studied military buildings anywhere. They were constructed by newcomers working in a region with its own long tradition of fortification, under conditions where a mistake meant losing the garrison, and the resulting designs record what those builders learned. The most obvious feature is concentric defence. An inner enclosure stands within an outer one, so an attacker who breaches the first wall enters a confined space overlooked from above rather than reaching the interior. This arrangement had appeared earlier in the region, notably in the great walls of the eastern capital, and the newcomers adopted it after encountering it rather than bringing it with them. Round towers replaced square ones for a specific reason. A square tower has corners that undermining can attack, and its faces leave dead ground that defenders cannot cover, whereas a rounded face deflects projectiles and can be watched from every angle. The change occurred across a few decades and spread back to Europe with returning builders. Water determined siting more than any other factor. A castle that could not hold water through a long siege would fall regardless of its walls, so cisterns cut into the rock occupy an enormous share of the interior volume at several sites, and the largest of these fortresses could support a garrison for a year. Their eventual capture rarely came through assault. Starvation, treachery, and negotiated surrender ended most sieges, since taking such a place by direct attack cost more than any commander wished to pay. What the ruins record is therefore a long argument, conducted in stone across two centuries, between engineers on both sides who studied each other closely.

subject: 다큐멘터리와 연출의 경계
title: How much shaping a true film may do
content: A documentary claims to show what happened, and yet every such film involves choices that shape what the audience concludes. Where the camera stands, what is cut, what music plays, and which order events appear in are all decisions, and none of them is neutral. The question is which of these choices are compatible with the claim to truth. Some are unavoidable. A film cannot show everything, so selection is required, and an unedited recording of many hours would not be more honest but merely unwatchable. Ordering material for clarity is likewise necessary, since the sequence in which things occurred is frequently less comprehensible than a reconstruction. Nobody regards these as deception. Other choices are contested. Asking a subject to repeat an action for the camera produces an image of something that did happen, staged for the recording, and traditions differ on whether this is acceptable. The earliest celebrated works in the form did exactly this, building sequences from arranged material while presenting them as observed, and the argument has continued ever since. Music is the most powerful and least examined. A score tells the audience how to feel about what they are watching, and it operates below the level at which viewers evaluate claims, so a film can present accurate footage while directing an emotional response the footage alone would not produce. Documentaries are rarely criticised for this, although the same technique in advertising would be called manipulation. What most practitioners settle on is a distinction between shaping and falsifying. Arranging true material so that its meaning is legible is the craft; producing an impression the maker knows to be false is the offence. The line is genuinely hard to hold, and the tradition's continuing arguments about particular films are arguments about exactly where it falls.

subject: 민요 수집과 변형
title: What happens when a song is written down
content: Collectors travelling through rural districts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries recorded songs that had circulated orally for generations. Their work preserved an enormous body of material that would otherwise have vanished, and it also transformed what it preserved, since writing a song down changes the thing being written. Oral songs exist in versions. A singer alters words to suit the occasion, forgets a verse, borrows a line from another song, and the result is a family of related performances with no original among them. A collector must choose one version to print, and the printed version then acquires an authority that no oral performance ever had, becoming the song against which later performances are measured. Collectors also edited. Verses considered coarse were removed or softened, texts were regularised into consistent metre, and tunes were fitted to standard notation that could not record the ornaments and rhythmic freedom the singers used. Several major collections were substantially rewritten by their compilers, and the extent of this was concealed at the time. Scholars unpicking such editions have found the collector's hand throughout. The purposes behind the collecting shaped the results. Many collectors were seeking evidence of a national spirit, so material that fitted that picture was gathered while songs learned from printed broadsides or from the music hall were dismissed as impure, even though rural singers sang them freely. The tradition as published is therefore narrower than the tradition as it existed. What followed was a genuine revival that returned these songs to performance, frequently in the edited forms, which then circulated back into oral use. The relationship between the archive and the living practice has been reciprocal ever since, and disentangling what was collected from what collection produced is now among the standard problems of the field.

subject: 개인 데이터는 누구의 것인가
title: Who owns the record of what you did
content: Records generated by a person's activity — where they went, what they bought, what they read — are held by whoever collected them. Calling these records the person's property seems natural, and the moral argument is more complicated than that framing suggests, since property is a poor fit for the thing in question. Ownership normally implies the right to transfer. If such records were property, a person could sell them outright, and afterwards they would have no further claim, which is precisely the arrangement that current practice already produces and that critics object to. Framing the issue as ownership therefore licenses the outcome it was meant to prevent. A second difficulty is that the records are jointly produced. A transaction involves two parties, a message involves a sender and a receiver, and a record of a hospital visit concerns the patient and the institution alike. Assigning exclusive ownership to one side misdescribes what generated the information. A more promising framing appeals to control rather than to ownership. What a person has a claim to is a say in how information about them is used, and that claim persists after the information has been shared, much as a confidence remains binding after it has been told. This treats the interest as ongoing rather than as something transferred once. A further consideration concerns aggregation. Individual records are frequently harmless while their combination reveals a great deal, so consent given piece by piece cannot address what the assembled picture makes possible. No individual transaction was objectionable, and yet the outcome is. What follows is that the moral vocabulary matters. Debating whether people own their data leads to markets in consent, whereas debating what may be done to a person with information about them leads somewhere else, and the second question is closer to what anybody actually cares about.

subject: 초기 영화가 회화에서 빌린 것
title: What the first films took from painting
content: When motion pictures began, no visual language for them existed. Filmmakers borrowed from what was available, and the available models were the theatre and painting, so the earliest work looks like a stage seen from a fixed seat and composed like a picture hung on a wall. The camera stood still and the actors arranged themselves within the frame. Composition followed painterly convention. Figures were balanced across the width, the important action occupied the centre, and depth was suggested by receding lines exactly as in a painted view. Directors with training in art applied it directly, and several early works reproduce well known paintings as tableaux, holding the arrangement long enough for the audience to recognise it. Lighting came from the same source. The dramatic side lighting of certain painting traditions was adopted for effect, and the practice of illuminating a face from one side while leaving the other in shadow entered film from the studio conventions of portraiture. Terms borrowed from painting remain in the vocabulary of cinematography. The break came with movement. Once the camera could move, and once cutting between shots became a technique rather than an accident, film gained a resource that painting did not have, and the borrowed compositions became limiting rather than useful. Directors began composing for a frame that would change, which is a different problem from composing a picture meant to be seen whole and at rest. The influence has run in both directions since. Painters absorbed the cropped, off centre framing that photography and film normalised, and the tradition of the arrested moment in painting has been shaped by images that audiences now read as film stills. Neither art has been independent of the other for well over a century.

subject: 박물관 조명이 유물에 하는 일
title: The light that shows and damages
content: Museums face a difficulty that has no solution, only a compromise. Objects must be lit to be seen, and light damages a great many of the materials they are made from, so every hour of display costs something that cannot be recovered. The conservation of a collection is partly a decision about how much of it to spend. The damage is cumulative and irreversible. Dyes fade, paper yellows, and organic material weakens, and the effect depends on total exposure rather than on intensity alone, so a low light maintained for years does as much harm as a bright one maintained briefly. This is why watercolours, textiles, and manuscripts are shown at levels that visitors find frustratingly dim, and why such objects are rotated out of display for long periods. The wavelengths matter as much as the quantity. Ultraviolet light is disproportionately destructive and contributes nothing to what the eye sees, so filtering it out is pure gain, and the shift to light sources that emit none has been the single greatest improvement available. Infrared produces heat, which brings its own problems for anything containing moisture. Display decisions therefore encode a judgment about audiences. An object lit brightly is seen well by many people now at the cost of being seen by fewer later, and different institutions weigh the present and future audience differently. Some have chosen to show facsimiles while keeping originals dark, which preserves the object and loses whatever presence the genuine thing supplies. The aesthetic consequences are considerable. Objects made to be seen by daylight or by candle are shown under conditions their makers never anticipated, and colours that were selected under one kind of light appear differently under another. What a visitor sees in a case is therefore always a modern interpretation, arrived at by curators balancing sight against survival.

subject: 티무르 왕조의 건축
title: Domes raised by a conqueror's descendants
content: The dynasty founded by Timur in the late fourteenth century built on an enormous scale across central Asia, and the buildings that survive in Samarkand and elsewhere define what most people picture when they imagine the architecture of that region. Their most recognisable feature is a ribbed dome on a high drum, sheathed in blue tile, and it is visible across a flat landscape from a great distance. This scale was deliberate, although it was occasionally excessive. One great mosque begun at the height of the empire was raised so rapidly and so ambitiously that parts began to fail almost immediately, and contemporary accounts describe bricks falling during prayers within a few years of completion. Because ambition outran the structural knowledge available, its walls needed constant repair, and this is a recurring pattern in the history of such building. The tile work of these buildings is their real technical achievement. Surfaces were covered with glazed pieces cut and fitted into patterns, and later with tiles painted in several colours and fired once, which was faster and permitted more complex designs. The blues came from cobalt and copper, and the intensity of the colour under strong sunlight was the effect intended. Craftsmen were brought from conquered regions, so the style itself records the empire's reach. These buildings served politics as much as religion. Raising a monument in a captured city announced who now ruled, and the tombs of the dynasty were made to be seen rather than to be entered. Later rulers of the same line carried the tradition into India, where it developed further and produced the buildings of the Mughal era. What survives has been heavily restored, although some of that work has been criticised by later specialists. Distinguishing medieval work from twentieth century reconstruction now requires expertise, which is a difficulty shared by many monuments that a modern state has adopted as a symbol.

subject: 풍자화가 정치에 미친 영향
title: Drawings that changed what people believed
content: Political cartoons occupy an odd position among the arts. They are made quickly, printed on cheap paper, and discarded, and yet several have altered the course of events in ways that carefully argued essays did not. Understanding why requires attending to how the form actually operates. A cartoon compresses an argument into an image that can be grasped in a second and remembered for years. Where an essay must establish its claims, a drawing asserts a relationship by placing two things in one frame, and the viewer supplies the connection themselves, which makes the conclusion feel like their own observation. This is the source of the form's power and of its dishonesty. Recurring symbols do much of the work. Once a tradition establishes that a particular animal represents a party, or a particular garment represents corruption, the artist can invoke the whole association with a stroke. Audiences learn this vocabulary from the drawings themselves, so the form teaches its readers how to read it and then relies on the training. The most celebrated campaigns were sustained. A nineteenth century American cartoonist attacked a corrupt city organisation week after week, and the organisation's leader is reported to have complained that his supporters could not read the newspapers but could certainly see the pictures. Whether that remark was ever made, the observation it contains is correct and has been exploited by every side since. The moral difficulty is that the technique works regardless of whether the target deserves it. Reducing a person to a caricature and repeating it makes the caricature what the public sees, and the same method that exposed genuine corruption has been used against minorities with devastating effect. Practitioners have generally located the limit at power, and the history of the form shows how frequently that limit has been ignored.

subject: 배심 제도가 지키는 것
title: Why ordinary people decide serious cases
content: Trial by a group of ordinary citizens is defended on grounds that have little to do with accuracy. Twelve people without legal training, hearing evidence once, are not obviously better at determining facts than an experienced judge would be, and yet many systems reserve their most serious cases for exactly this arrangement. The reasons are worth examining. The oldest justification concerns power. A jury stands between the state and the accused, and it cannot be dismissed, promoted, or pressured in the way that an official can, so a prosecution requires the assent of people with no career at stake. Historical episodes in which juries refused to convict under laws they regarded as unjust are cited on both sides of the argument, since the same independence that protects can also nullify. A second justification concerns legitimacy. A verdict reached by fellow citizens carries an authority that an official's decision does not, and the community that must live with the outcome participated in reaching it. This matters more where trust in institutions is thin, which is precisely where criminal justice is hardest to sustain. A third concerns the standard applied. Deciding whether conduct was reasonable, or whether a doubt is reasonable, calls for community judgment rather than technical expertise, and a group drawn from the population is arguably better placed to supply it than a specialist whose experience is unrepresentative. The objections are serious. Juries are affected by presentation, they cannot be asked to explain themselves, and research on their reasoning is restricted almost everywhere. Complex financial cases strain them badly. What the defence finally rests on is that the alternative concentrates the decision in officials, and that a system valuing constraint on state power has reason to accept some loss of accuracy in exchange.

subject: 건축의 폐허 미학
title: Buildings admired for being broken
content: A taste for ruins developed in European art during the eighteenth century and has never entirely disappeared. Painters composed views of broken arches overgrown with vegetation, landowners built artificial ruins in their grounds, and travellers sought out the remains of ancient buildings in preference to intact ones. This preference requires explanation, since a ruin is a failure of the thing it once was. Part of the appeal was temporal. A ruin makes the passage of time visible in a way that a maintained building does not, and it presents the viewer with evidence that the civilization which built it has ended. Writers of the period described the resulting feeling as pleasurable melancholy, and the aesthetic sits close to the sublime, since what is being contemplated is the scale of what has been lost. A second element was formal. Time removes the roof, opens the walls, and lets vegetation in, producing irregular shapes and unexpected framings that no architect would design. The broken building becomes picturesque in the specific sense the era used, meaning that it composes well as a picture, and painters valued exactly the qualities that a builder would have regarded as damage. The taste had consequences for conservation. When such buildings began to be protected, a dispute arose that has never been settled: whether to stabilise a ruin as a ruin, preserving the state that is admired, or to restore what was lost. Restoring destroys the object of the aesthetic, and leaving alone eventually destroys the building. The argument runs through nineteenth century architectural debate and continues in current practice. Modern versions of the taste attach to industrial buildings, and photographs of abandoned factories circulate widely. Critics describe such work as aestheticising the collapse of livelihoods, which is a serious charge and one that the eighteenth century admirers of classical ruins never had to answer.

subject: 초기 인쇄물의 삽화와 문해
title: Pictures printed for readers who could not read
content: The first century of printing produced a great many books illustrated with woodcuts, and the pictures were not decoration. Literacy was limited, texts were expensive, and a printed sheet frequently reached an audience who could take in the image while somebody else read the words aloud. The relationship between the two elements was designed with that audience in mind. Woodcut suited the technology exactly. Because a cut block is relief printed like type, image and text could be locked into the same forme and printed together in one pass, which made illustration cheap. Engraved plates produce finer lines and required a separate printing, so they remained expensive and were used differently. This technical fact determined which books were illustrated and how heavily. The images were reused freely. A printer owning a stock of blocks would employ the same figure to represent different people in different books, and the same city view might serve for several cities within a single volume. Readers accepted this, which indicates that the pictures were understood as indicating a kind rather than depicting a particular, much as a diagram works now. Certain genres depended on illustration entirely. Herbals, anatomical works, and manuals of craft could not convey their content in words alone, and the history of scientific illustration begins with the recognition that a printed image is identical in every copy while a hand copied drawing degrades. This reliability, rather than beauty, was what changed the transmission of technical knowledge. Cheap printed sheets carrying a large image and a few lines of text reached the widest audience of all. They carried news, moral instruction, and political attack, and they were pasted on walls where those who could not read learned their contents from the picture. Almost none survive, since nobody preserved them, and what is known comes from the few that were bound into collections by accident.

subject: 향과 냄새의 문화적 코드
title: An art that works on a sense we barely discuss
content: Every culture attaches meanings to particular smells, and yet smell is the sense least served by aesthetic vocabulary. There is no notation, no established critical tradition, and no museum that displays scent as its principal material, which makes the cultural practices built around it unusually difficult to study. The associations are learned rather than natural. A scent that one tradition uses in worship may be used in another for cooking, and responses that feel instinctive turn out to differ across populations. Incense burned in a religious setting acquires its meaning from that setting, and somebody who encountered the same resin first in a market forms a different association entirely. The apparent immediacy of the response conceals a history. Memory is the source of the sense's peculiar power. Smell reaches the parts of the brain concerned with memory and emotion by a shorter route than the other senses, which is the standard explanation for why a scent can recover a scene from decades earlier with unusual force. Writers have described the effect for centuries, and perfumers exploit it deliberately by building compositions around materials associated with childhood or with particular places. Perfumery is the closest thing to a formal art of the sense. Its practitioners work with a vocabulary of families and structures, compositions unfold over time as different components evaporate, and the tradition has its own canon and its own arguments about originality. It has nonetheless been treated as a trade rather than an art, partly because its products are sold commercially and partly because the results cannot be exhibited or archived reliably. Materials degrade, formulas are altered when ingredients become unavailable, and a scent composed a century ago cannot now be smelled as it was. Whatever tradition exists is therefore preserved less securely than in any other art.

subject: 스와힐리 해안의 도시들
title: Stone towns facing the monsoon
content: Along the eastern coast of Africa, from Somalia down to Mozambique, stand the remains of towns built in coral stone from the medieval centuries onward. They were commercial cities, oriented toward the ocean rather than toward the interior, and their prosperity depended on a wind that reverses twice a year. The monsoon made the trade possible. Ships could sail from Arabia and India to this coast in one season and return in the other, which meant that merchants stayed for months, and the towns developed to accommodate that pattern. Goods from the interior — gold, ivory, timber, and people — were exchanged for cloth, ceramics, and beads, and Chinese porcelain recovered from these sites demonstrates how far the network reached. The civilization that developed was neither African with foreign additions nor a colony of Arabia, and older scholarship insisting on one of those readings has been discarded. The language belongs to an African family while carrying substantial borrowed vocabulary, the architecture uses local materials with forms found across the ocean world, and the population was drawn from both directions over centuries of intermarriage. Excavation has shown continuous occupation from before the arrival of Islam, which settles a question that colonial era writers had answered incorrectly. The towns competed rather than combined. Each was independent, ruled by its own leading families, and their rivalry is recorded in chronicles that survive from several of them. This independence made them vulnerable when Portuguese fleets arrived at the end of the fifteenth century, since no combined resistance was possible. Several were sacked, trade routes were redirected, and the coast declined. What remains is a chain of ruined towns, several with standing mosques and tombs, along with living cities whose older quarters preserve the same building tradition.

subject: 이유란 무엇인가
title: What it is for something to count in favour
content: When we say that somebody had a reason to act, we mean that some consideration counted in favour of acting. This notion sits underneath most moral thinking, and yet saying what a reason actually is turns out to be surprisingly hard, because two quite different things are called by the same word. One kind explains. If we say that a person's reason for leaving was that they felt unwelcome, we are describing what moved them, whether or not the feeling was justified. The other kind justifies. If we say they had reason to leave, we are claiming that something genuinely counted in favour of it, regardless of whether they noticed. The two come apart constantly, and confusing them produces argument at cross purposes. A further question concerns what makes something a reason of the second kind. One tradition holds that reasons derive from what a person wants, so a consideration counts in favour only if it connects to some existing motive. This explains how reasons move people, since the connection to motivation is built in. It has the uncomfortable consequence that somebody who wants nothing good has no reason to behave well. The opposing tradition holds that some considerations count independently of what anybody wants. Suffering supplies a reason to relieve it whether or not the person addressed cares, and this fits our practice of criticising the indifferent. Its difficulty is explaining how such a reason connects to action in somebody who is unmoved. What the dispute clarifies is that moral argument depends on the second tradition being at least partly right. Telling somebody they ought to act differently is pointless if reasons reach only as far as existing desires, and the whole practice of moral persuasion presupposes that considerations can count for a person who has not yet recognised them.

subject: 자수와 여성 노동의 기록
title: Stitched sheets as a record of work
content: Historians studying the daily labour of women before the twentieth century face a shortage of sources. Records were kept about property, taxation, and litigation, and those documents mention women mainly as they relate to men. Needlework survives in quantity from the same centuries, and it has increasingly been read as evidence rather than only as decoration. Practice pieces are the most informative. Sheets worked by girls learning the craft carry alphabets, numerals, and rows of stitches, frequently signed with a name and an age, and sometimes with a place. Assembled in quantity they record how old girls were when they began, what they were taught, in what order, and how the curriculum differed between households, charity schools, and orphanages. No written source supplies this. The finished objects record economic activity as well. Where a household produced work for sale, the volume and the quality indicate what the labour was worth, and inventories occasionally list such items alongside other assets. In several regions this work supplied a substantial share of household income while appearing in no occupational record, since the women doing it were described as having no employment. Some pieces carry text deliberately. Verses about mortality, obedience, and industry appear frequently, chosen by whoever was supervising, so the objects also record what girls were being taught to think. Occasionally a maker departed from the assigned text, and those departures have attracted particular attention from historians looking for evidence of what the makers themselves felt. The methodological difficulty is that survival was selective. Fine work by prosperous households was kept and framed while ordinary mending was used until it disintegrated, so the record over represents leisure and under represents necessity. Any conclusion drawn from these materials has to account for that filter, which is the same problem that affects every other kind of surviving object.

subject: 도시 광장의 조각과 기억
title: How a square arranges what people notice
content: A public square is a designed space, and the sculpture placed in it works together with that design rather than standing independently. Where an object sits, what a person sees on approaching, and whether they must walk around it or past it are decisions that determine how much attention it receives and what relation the viewer takes up. Placing a work at the centre asserts that the square exists around it. Everything else becomes background, sightlines converge, and the object cannot be avoided by anybody crossing. This arrangement was standard for the equestrian monuments of earlier centuries, and the resulting relation is straightforwardly hierarchical: the viewer looks up at a figure that occupies the ground everybody else must move around. Placing a work at the edge produces something else entirely. It is encountered rather than confronted, it competes with whatever else occupies the space, and people who use the square daily may stop noticing it. Designers frequently prefer this for contemporary commissions, since an object at the edge invites approach rather than deference, and can be examined closely instead of being seen from a fixed distance. The ground matters as much as the object. A raised plinth separates and elevates; setting a work at pavement level places it among the people using the space, which is why removing a plinth has become a deliberate gesture. Some recent commissions are set into the paving, so that visitors walk across rather than around. What follows is that arguments about public sculpture are frequently arguments about arrangement rather than about the work itself. A figure that reads as domineering on a plinth in the centre may read quite differently at the edge and at eye level, and cities revisiting contested monuments have sometimes found that moving a work accomplishes more than removing it.

subject: 증거와 믿음의 관계
title: How far belief should follow the evidence
content: A familiar principle holds that it is wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence. The claim was stated forcefully in the nineteenth century using the example of a shipowner who convinces himself that his vessel is sound, sends it to sea, and drowns the passengers, and the argument is that he is guilty whether or not the ship happens to sink. The reasoning behind the principle is not merely about consequences. Belief guides action, so somebody who believes carelessly is prepared to act carelessly, and the fact that they escaped harm on one occasion says nothing about the practice. There is also a claim about what we owe each other, since a person forming beliefs badly pollutes a shared resource of testimony that everybody depends upon. The opposing tradition argues that the principle is too strict. Some questions must be decided before the evidence can be complete, and refusing to believe until it is amounts to deciding in the negative by default. Where a belief is itself part of what makes an outcome possible — trust in a colleague, confidence in a project — demanding prior evidence forecloses the very thing that would have supplied it. A moderate position distinguishes contexts. Where a belief will guide action affecting others, the demand for evidence is stringent, and the shipowner fails it plainly. Where a belief concerns one's own life, cannot be settled by available evidence, and must be decided one way or another, more latitude is defensible. What both sides accept is that belief is not entirely voluntary, which complicates the moral vocabulary. We cannot simply decide to believe, so any obligation must attach to how we gather evidence and how we handle what we find, which relocates the duty from the belief itself to the inquiry that produced it.

subject: 차와 커피가 만든 사교 공간
title: Rooms built around a drink
content: The arrival of tea and coffee in Europe during the seventeenth century produced a new kind of public room. Establishments serving these drinks differed from taverns in a specific respect: the beverage did not intoxicate, so conversation could continue for hours without deteriorating, and the rooms attracted people who came to talk rather than to drink. The social arrangements that developed were distinctive. Admission cost very little, seating was communal, and newspapers and pamphlets were provided, so a man of modest means could sit alongside people he would never otherwise meet. Particular houses acquired particular clienteles — merchants in one, writers in another, men of science in a third — and several institutions that still exist began as regular gatherings in such rooms. An insurance market and more than one learned society trace their origin to a coffee house. The cultural effect was contested at the time. Authorities regarded the rooms with suspicion, since discussion of public affairs among people of no particular standing was exactly what they wished to discourage, and attempts were made to close them. Others complained that the establishments wasted time and encouraged idle talk, which is a complaint made about every new social space since. Tea developed differently, becoming domestic rather than public in Britain, and the ceremony that grew around it was organised by women within the household rather than by men in a room outside it. The same substance therefore produced opposite social forms depending on where it was consumed, which indicates that the arrangements were cultural rather than following from the drink. What both traditions demonstrate is how a commodity can generate an institution. Neither the coffee house nor the tea table existed before the material arrived, and both outlasted the novelty of the drink itself to become settled parts of how a culture arranged its sociability.
